Asked an engineer friend:

"Why do engineers who have the ability to switch jobs, stay in environments that are dysfunctional?"

Answer:

"As long as it isn't unbearable, we assume the next place will be the same. Plus, with creativity, you can make any job fun."

Thoughts?
Once you realize that 95% of prioritization frameworks are negotiation frameworks under the guise of objectivity it all becomes easier.

Don’t bring me problems, bring me solutions is often code for “don’t remind me of the mess we’re in or how we got this way, just make the problem go away”

The crux issue is that without that core acceptance, progress is very hard.

No joke,  @atlassian Atlas is one of the most promising product products I’ve seen in a while. It’ll probably appeal to 5% of teams in the world who are ok with how opinionated and “simple” it is, but it works.

(I have absolutely no connection to @Atlassian )
The best approach to managing tech debt is making sure to move jobs every couple years and get hired to do green field work each time.
Long time coming but a while ago I asked Twitter to help define "Product Thinking". I finally got around to grouping the 120 odd responses...

a whole generation of new PMs assuming product management is a combination of 1) learning frameworks, 2) leadership porn and mini-founder-ism, and 3) being "top N%" to get ahead

troubling...
"I’m not sure we need to optimize the speed of producing mediocre work" @jmspool

"explain the cognitive biases at play that would lead to a product manager shipping a feature to get immediate value over improving the whole system of delivery that could increase throughput by 2x.

Describe their inner narrative with biases marked in parenthesis."

Is it me, or are there more and more PMs advancing into leadership roles without a sound understanding of how businesses work and the commercial side?

Like they’ve spent more time trying to do UX and focus on delivery.

May be way off.
